summary: Summarizes the current uses of the offer/answer model in SIP communication. SIP uses it with SDP to set up and change multimedia sessions, but the description was spread across many RFCs. This informational document gathers it together.

eli5.summary: Starting a call is like one person offering a way to talk and the other saying yes or suggesting changes. This gathers into one place all the rules about how that back-and-forth works in SIP.

subtitle: How SIP establishes and updates multimedia sessions using offers and answers

tldr.problem: SIP calls need a standardized way to negotiate multimedia capabilities (audio, video, codecs) when setting up and changing sessions. The offer/answer model rules were scattered across multiple RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: One party sends an offer describing what it can do; the other sends an answer confirming acceptance, rejection, or counter-proposal. This document gathers all the ways this exchange can happen in SIP into one place.
tldr.outcome: Developers and operators can implement SIP correctly and avoid the subtle bugs that occur when offers and answers collide or when the same negotiation happens via different SIP methods.

facts.label: Maximum offer/answer exchanges
facts.value: One per dialog at a time

today: RFC 6337 is Informational and was published in August 2011. It clarifies the existing offer/answer rules in SIP but does not make normative changes to the RFCs it summarizes. SIP implementations still rely on RFC 3261, RFC 3262, RFC 3264, and RFC 6141 as the authoritative sources, using this document as a reference for understanding the overall picture.

sections.title: What Offers and Answers Are
sections.content:
SIP establishes and updates multimedia sessions by having one party send an offer describing what it can do (media types, codecs, bandwidth) and the other party send an answer confirming or rejecting those choices. This offer/answer model is defined in RFC 3264 in abstract terms. The challenge is that SIP has many ways to send an offer and answer across multiple messages and methods, and the rules are spread across several RFCs. This document brings them together.

Only certain session descriptions in SIP messages are valid offers or answers. Not every SDP (Session Description Protocol) body is one—some are just capability reports or confirmations. At any moment, exactly one offer/answer negotiation can be in progress in a single SIP dialog.
sections.eli5: Think of a contract negotiation: you send a proposal, they send an acceptance or counter-offer. This explains all the different ways to do that in SIP conversations, so everyone stays synchronized.

sections.title: The Six Offer/Answer Exchange Patterns
sections.content:
SIP defines exactly six patterns for exchanging offers and answers across different request and response types:

Pattern 1: Offer in INVITE request → Answer in 2xx response. Pattern 2: Offer in 2xx response → Answer in ACK request. Both let a caller or callee make the initial proposal.

Patterns 3 and 4 use the 100rel extension for reliable provisional responses. Pattern 3 puts the offer in INVITE; Pattern 4 puts it in a provisional 1xx response and the answer in a PRACK acknowledgment. These let a UAS (server) respond early and let the offer/answer exchange complete before the final response.

Pattern 5: A PRACK request can carry a new offer after confirming a provisional response that contained an answer. Pattern 6: An UPDATE request lets either party propose changes in an early or established dialog without using INVITE. Each pattern has rules about who can use it and when rejections are allowed.
sections.eli5: There are six different ways to hand over proposals in SIP: through INVITE and responses, early provisional responses with special acknowledgments, and the UPDATE method. Each one has strengths and weaknesses depending on whether you're setting up a call or changing it mid-conversation.

sections.title: Handling Collisions and Race Conditions
sections.content:
Two problems can arise when both parties want to change the session at the same time. Message crossing occurs when an answer is delayed: party A sends offer 1, party B receives offer 2 before sending the answer to offer 1. The RFC defines rules to ensure A detects that offer 2 is not the answer to offer 1. Glare is worse: both parties send offers at nearly the same time. Each one receives the other's offer before its own answer arrives.

SIP prevents glare by making certain offers (via UPDATE or re-INVITE) fail with response code 491 if one is already in progress. The sender waits and retries. For PRACK, which must always succeed with a 200 response, there is a tension that the document highlights: the code always succeeds but there may be no good way to signal that an offer in a PRACK cannot be accepted. The document provides detailed guidance on which methods prevent which race conditions and how to implement the state machine correctly.
sections.eli5: When both sides try to renegotiate at once, SIP needs special rules to avoid confusion. It rejects duplicate proposals or makes one side wait and try again, so both ends stay in sync.

sections.title: What Goes in Offers and Answers
sections.content:
A UA sending an offer should include the media types and codecs it is ready to use right then—not just what it is capable of in theory. A UA answering an offer must include the same number of media lines as the offer and either accept them (with a port number) or reject them (with port zero). The answer can add extra formats that are also in the offer, but this creates an asymmetric situation and should be done rarely.

When sending a new offer in response to an offer-less request, the offerer should offer all the media types and codecs it wants to use at that moment, not just the ones from previous negotiations. This lets the parties renegotiate to use video again if they had agreed to audio-only earlier. The hold and resume feature is important: sendonly and recvonly attributes indicate whether a stream is on hold without being rejected, and the rules for changing these states are subtle.
sections.eli5: An offer is like saying what equipment you have available right now, and an answer says which parts you can use and how. If you need to pause the video but keep the call, there's a special way to say that.

sections.title: When Offers Can and Cannot Change
sections.content:
Once an offer/answer exchange is complete, the next offer must follow strict rules. The 'o=' line version number must increment by exactly one; if it does not change, the entire SDP must be identical. The number of media lines cannot shrink; rejected lines must stay and can be reused. For RTP, the mapping from a payload type to a codec within a media stream must not change during the session. These constraints prevent subtle interoperability failures.

If a re-INVITE fails after media has already been exchanged using the new offer, RFC 3261 says to roll back to the old state, but this is hard in practice. RFC 6141 recommends that a UAS send a 2xx response with a syntactically valid answer in this case rather than reject, preserving the session. The document provides detailed guidance on which scenarios require rolling back and when a UA should send a successful answer even if the offer is not ideal.
sections.eli5: Once you agree on how to talk, both sides have to remember what they agreed to and follow those rules. You can't suddenly use a codec you didn't agree on, and you have to account for all the streams you set up, even the ones on hold.
